subject: Time complexity of HMC algorithm used in stan

messages.author: 77e72e34bf8c033f
messages.subject: Time complexity of HMC algorithm used in stan
parts:
Hi all

Is the time complexity of the HMC algo used in stan known? I recently got alot more data points and experienced that the runtime (naive runtime, have not looked at ESS/time) dramatically increased, more than linear in the number of data points. So I am wondering if I can expect some kind of behavior, like O(N_data)? Or maybe this is too dependent on the specific data and model?

Thx for an awesome piece of software!

Per

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Time complexity of HMC algorithm used in stan
parts:
Too dependent on the exact geometry of the posterior.

The basic cost per transition is cost(gradient) * N_leapfrog steps,
where cost(gradient) will depend on your exact model — it often
scales linearly with the data, but not always, and the scaling 
with respect to parameters depends sensitively on your model.
Then N_leapfrog steps scales as integration_time / step_size,
where integrate_time and step_size depend very sensitivity
on the geometry of the posterior.  

Heavy tails?  Integration time goes way up.
Strong constraints from data?  Step size goes way down.
Etc, etc, etc.

Best you can do is try an empirical study, where you vary
the data in your specific model and see you if you can
identify a natural scaling.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Time complexity of HMC algorithm used in stan
parts:
> On Jun 3, 2015, at 5:00 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Too dependent on the exact geometry of the posterior.
>
> The basic cost per transition is cost(gradient) * N_leapfrog steps,
> where cost(gradient) will depend on your exact model — it often
> scales linearly with the data, but not always,

The scaling is with the number of edges in the expression graph
for simple expressions (which is the number of operands used in
functions and operators) --- things like ode solvers can take longer
because they're encapsulating iterative algorithms that depend on
state, much like HMC itself. Sometimes the number of edges scales
more than linearly in the data, for instance in a GP.

- Bob
